History & Physical (Detailed)

Consult Summary:
48-year-old man with asthma presents with a 3-day history of watery diarrhoea, peri-umbilical abdominal pain and one episode of vomiting; clinical picture most consistent with acute infectious gastroenteritis.

History:
• Presenting complaint: Persistent watery diarrhoea for 3 days.  
• Onset/Timeline: Began abruptly 3 days ago; frequency every ~10 min, no improvement or worsening reported.  
• Abdominal pain: Central, just below umbilicus; mild-to-moderate; partially relieved after bowel motion; mild tenderness on self-palpation.  
• Vomiting: Single episode this morning after eating fruit (strawberries); no haematemesis.  
• Nausea: Intermittent.  
• Bowel characteristics: No visible blood.  
• Hydration/Nutrition: Limiting oral intake; unsure if drinking enough fluids.  
• Fever: Denies clear fever; mild sweating over past 4 days.  
• Respiratory: Baseline asthma; no new dyspnoea, no chest pain.  
• Functional impact: Unable to work; needs close access to toilet.  
• Red-flag review: No weight loss, no rectal bleeding, no severe or radiating abdominal pain.

Past Medical History:
• Asthma – stable; uses inhaler; no recent exacerbations reported.

Medications:
• Unspecified inhaler for asthma (dose/route/frequency not documented); recent change in brand.  
Allergies:
• NKDA (No known drug allergies).

Social History:
• Currently staying home from work due to symptoms.  
• Smoking, alcohol, recreational drugs: not discussed.  
• Reports anxiety at times (contextual).

Family History:
• Father died of bowel (colorectal) cancer ~10 years ago.

Physical Examination:
• Vitals: Not recorded.  
• Abdomen: Patient-reported mild central tenderness; no localisation, guarding or rebound reported.  
• Other systems: Not examined in the consult.

Investigations:
• None performed during tele-consult.

Assessment & Plan:
Overall Impression:
Acute infectious gastroenteritis (likely viral) causing watery diarrhoea, mild abdominal cramps and single vomiting episode, with low concern for surgical abdomen or colorectal malignancy at present.

DDx Integration (key items)
1. Acute viral gastroenteritis – sudden onset, watery stool, mild pain, brief vomiting, no blood or high fever.  
2. Bacterial food-borne gastroenteritis – similar picture; less likely given absence of fever or dysentery.  
3. Colorectal carcinoma – family history raises long-term risk; acute presentation and lack of red flags make current episode unlikely related.

Issue 1 – Acute gastroenteritis / dehydration risk
• Advise oral hydration: water, oral rehydration salts if available.  
• Light diet as tolerated (bland foods).  
• Observe for red flags: persistent vomiting preventing oral intake, fever ≥38 °C, bloody stool, severe worsening pain, signs of dehydration.  
• Medication: No antibiotics recommended at this stage.  
• Sick note/work advice: Stay off work until 48 h after symptom resolution to reduce transmission.  
• Safety-net: If symptoms worsen or not improving within 24–48 h, attend in-person GP assessment; seek emergency care for red flags.

Issue 2 – Asthma (chronic)
• Continue regular inhaler use; ensure adequate supply.  
• Monitor control; seek review if increased usage or wheeze develops.

Issue 3 – Family history of colorectal cancer / patient anxiety
• Reassured low likelihood that current acute illness is cancer-related.  
• Advised future routine colorectal cancer screening per national guidelines (discuss with GP at next visit).  
• Offered GP follow-up to address ongoing concerns.

General plan items
• Provide written self-care and red-flag information.  
• Follow-up: Tele-review if no improvement in 48 h or sooner if deterioration.

Quality checks:
• Missing elements: Objective vitals, full abdominal exam, smoking/alcohol history, complete medication list.  
• Conflicts: None noted between transcript and DDx.  
• Transcript quality: Clear audio; no major inaudible portions.
